## Purpose

`integration_develop` puts a project into **development** delivery mode and
records the policy that mode runs under. Development mode is the lightweight
publisher: it assembles completed task branches into one batch with ordinary Git,
runs the operator's own validation commands locally, and pushes the result to the
default branch with a lease. There is no GitHub App, no attestation service, no
CI receipt and no synthetic review evidence — the guide calls this out explicitly
([`src/integration/development.py:1`](../../../src/integration/development.py)).

The policy this command stores is small and total: how to validate
(`focused` with at least one command, `advisory`, or `none`), which commands to
run, how long they may take, how often to sweep, and how many sources one batch
may carry. Changing that policy is the same call — it is a configuration write,
not a toggle. See the
[integration operation model](README.md#the-integration-operation-model) and
[development integration](../../guides/development-integration.md).

## When a playbook uses it

It is an operator command: `_cmd_integration_develop`
([`src/commands/integration_commands.py:1743`](../../../src/commands/integration_commands.py))
requires a LOCAL principal, so a project playbook is refused `unauthorized`. The
real entry point is `aq integration develop PROJECT_ID --validation … --command …
--reason …` ([`src/cli/integration.py:217`](../../../src/cli/integration.py)),
which assembles the `policy` object from flags.

A playbook's use is confined to local installation or onboarding routines that
run as the daemon itself. Everything a playbook would want afterwards —
requesting a sweep — is [`integration_flush`](integration_flush.md), which needs
no operator authority.

## How it works internally

1. The contract is generated by the shared development registration
   ([`src/commands/contracts/integration.py:1946`](../../../src/commands/contracts/integration.py)),
   so it carries the whole `_DEVELOPMENT_OUTCOMES` vocabulary even though this
   command only ever produces `configured` or `blocked`.
2. `_cmd_integration_develop` (line 1743) requires a LOCAL principal and passes
   that principal's description as `operator_id`. `ValueError`, `RuntimeError`
   and `KeyError` from the service are all mapped to `blocked` with the message.
3. `DevelopmentIntegration.configure`
   ([`src/integration/development.py:866`](../../../src/integration/development.py))
   validates the policy through `DevelopmentPolicy` (line 29), which forbids
   unknown keys and rejects `focused` validation with no commands, then requires a
   non-empty reason.
4. It resolves the repository. An explicitly designated
   `integration_repository_id` wins. Otherwise the project must have exactly one
   registered repository — and if it has none, the command will discover an
   `origin` remote from the project's registered checkout, resolve a relative
   filesystem origin against that checkout, and register it. Zero or multiple
   repositories after all that is an error.
5. Under the repository exclusion lock and the project lock, in-flight writes to
   the default branch must have settled: any `integration_promotion_intents` row
   for that branch not yet `committed`, `conflict` or `superseded` blocks the
   switch, because two publishers must never overlap.
6. The project is switched to `development` with the validated policy, legacy
   suppression and branch-owner state are reconciled for the new publisher, the
   next sweep is scheduled at `now + interval_seconds`, and a
   `development_deliveries` row is written in state `adopted` whose evidence
   records the operator and the policy — so the configuration change is itself
   part of the delivery journal.

## Side effects and persistence

The project row's integration mode, policy and designated repository
([`src/database/tables.py:37`](../../../src/database/tables.py)); possibly one new
row in `repos` when an origin had to be discovered; one journal row in
`development_deliveries` (line 3839) with `state: adopted` and
`evidence.kind: configuration`; and the in-memory next-due time for the project's
sweep.

Switching modes does not rewrite history. Rows left by a previous publisher stay
as audit history, and a batch that was mid-flight under the old mode is what the
pre-switch settle check is protecting.

## Failure modes and diagnostics

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `configured` | The project is in development mode with this policy. |
| `blocked` | The service refused. The message names why. |
| `unauthorized` | The caller is not a LOCAL operator. |

`blocked` covers every refusal, so read the message:

- `validation must be focused, advisory, or none` / `focused validation requires
  at least one local command` — the policy is invalid.
- `configuration reason is required` — `--reason` was blank.
- `project not found`, `project repository needs a remote URL`, or `designate a
  repository when the project has zero or multiple repositories` — repository
  resolution failed.
- A pending default-branch promotion intent — an older publisher has not settled;
  let it finish or resolve it before switching.

Confirm the result with `aq integration status PROJECT_ID`, which reports the
effective mode and the delivery receipts development mode writes. The remaining
per-sweep behaviour is documented on
[`integration_development_sweep`](integration_development_sweep.md).

## Example step

```markdown
1. Call `integration_develop` with `project_id` `agent-queue`, `reason` `local
   delivery for the pilot project`, and `policy` `{"validation": "focused",
   "commands": ["aq test tests/test_smoke.py"], "interval_seconds": 300}`. A
   `configured` outcome ends the rule; a `blocked`, `unauthorized`, `rejected` or
   `runtime_error` outcome fails it.
```
